implementation_notes: POSIX provides the primitives: the acceptor is a listening descriptor (socket -> bind -> listen) consumed with accept(); on Linux, accept4() can set SOCK_NONBLOCK|SOCK_CLOEXEC atomically, while portable POSIX code uses accept() followed by fcntl(). The connector role is connect(), which in non-blocking mode completes asynchronously via select/poll with SO_ERROR. The handler factory, activation hook and dispatcher integration are hand-written C. Never read/write the listening descriptor; hand the accepted descriptor to the handler and register it with the demultiplexer (epoll/select/poll).
pitfalls: Blocking accept() in a single-threaded loop stalls every other connection; use non-blocking descriptors plus select/poll/epoll or a dedicated accept thread.
Missing FD_CLOEXEC/SOCK_CLOEXEC leaks listening or connected descriptors across exec; set close-on-exec on every descriptor you create.
EINTR must be retried; portability requires checking both EAGAIN and EWOULDBLOCK.
Non-blocking connect() does not block the caller but reports completion via select/poll with SO_ERROR; forgetting to check SO_ERROR means a failed connect goes silent.
The listen backlog (second argument to listen()) is only a hint — the kernel may cap it; size it with expected concurrency and test overload behaviour.
